title: "TTpipe"

description: "An annotated tour of the lab's TT-seq pipeline: switches, conditional rules, target functions and tests that count jobs."
---

TTpipe is the largest of the three pipelines: seven rule files plus `common.smk`, 33 rule
definitions (a few are two variants of one rule), and a config with switches that turn whole halves of the workflow on and off. It is the place to see module 6
(structure) and module 8 (testing) at full size.

Code on this page is pulled from the repository at the pinned commit (ebdc210), and each
block links to the same lines on GitHub. Line numbers in the text are the file's own line numbers.

## What the pipeline does {#tt-biology}

TT-seq measures transcription as it happens. Cells are given 4-thiouridine (4sU) for a short pulse,
so only RNA made during those minutes carries the label. The labeled RNA is fragmented and pulled
down, and the library is sequenced strand-specifically. Because most of that RNA is freshly made
and not yet spliced, reads cover introns as well as exons, and the signal reflects how much
polymerase passed through a gene during the pulse rather than how much mature RNA has piled up.
TTpipe reimplements the TT-seq workflow described for Magnitov et al. 2024 (*Mol Cell*, GEO
GSE260914); the shipped samplesheet describes that study's eight mouse ES cell samples (ZFP143
degradation: DMSO, 2 h, 6 h, 24 h, two replicates each), with paths you replace.

Processing aligns read pairs with STAR, keeps reads with MAPQ ≥ 10, removes PCR duplicates with
Picard, and splits each BAM into the two genomic strands. Replicates of a condition are merged and
turned into scaled bigWig tracks, and HTSeq counts reads over whole gene bodies on each strand.
Analysis runs DESeq2 for every comparison against a reference condition, ranks genes for
preranked GSEA (fgsea), and draws a Sankey diagram of how genes move between up, down and
unchanged across the comparisons. Reports summarize QC, strandedness and replicate agreement.

## The rule graph {#tt-rulegraph}

{{< generated name="ttpipe-rulegraph" >}}


The graph has two halves joined at the count matrix. Processing runs from `fastqc` and `star_align`
down to `bigwig` and `count_matrix`; analysis runs from `count_matrix` (or a matrix you supply) and
`sample_table` through `deseq2`, `rnk`, `fgsea` and `sankey`. The report rules (`qc_summary`,
`qc_report`, `multiqc`, `results_explorer`, `stranded_signal`) hang off both. Which boxes exist
depends on the config: with `trim: true` there is a `fastp` box, with `gsea_collections` set there are
`rnk` and `fgsea` boxes, and with `run_processing: false` the whole top half is gone.

The repository keeps its own diagrams in `docs/img/`, and `tests/test_dag.py` fails when they no
longer match `snakemake --rulegraph`, so they cannot drift from the code.

On the test fixture (2 conditions × 2 replicates) the full dry run plans 60 jobs, among them
4 `star_align`, 8 `fastqc` (two mates × four samples), 8 `split_strands` and 8 `htseq_count` (two
strands × four samples), and 6 `bigwig` (two conditions × all/forward/reverse).

## A walk from inputs to outputs {#tt-walk}

1. **`samplesheet.txt`**: one row per sample with `Name`, `Condition`, `Replicate`, and the FASTQ
   columns (only needed when processing runs).
2. **`config/TTpipeConfig.yaml`**: the switches (`run_processing`, `run_analysis`, `qc_report`, `trim`,
   `multiqc`, `spike_in`), the reference, strandedness, and the DESeq2/GSEA settings.
3. **`workflows/rules/common.smk`** reads both, checks them, and defines every output path as a
   template plus the target functions.
4. **Per sample**: `fastqc` → (`fastp`) → `star_align` → `mapq_filter` → `mark_duplicates` →
   `split_strands` → `htseq_count`.
5. **Per condition**: `merge_bams` → `scale_factors` → `bigwig`.
6. **Once**: `gene_info`, `count_matrix`, `sample_table`, `deseq2`, `sankey`, the reports.
7. **Per comparison and gene-set collection**: `rnk` → `fgsea`.

## Concepts in the wild

### The samplesheet as an input {#tt-sample-table}

This is the most instructive rule in the three pipelines, because it records a bug that happened.

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/TTpipe.snakefile" lines="35-50" >}}

`sample_table` writes the sample/condition/replicate table DESeq2 reads. The `run:` block takes the
values from `SAMPLES` and `SAMPLE_TABLE`, which `common.smk` built from the samplesheet when the
Snakefile was parsed. So the rule does not need to *read* the samplesheet. It lists it as input
anyway, and the comment says why: without it, adding samples to the sheet did not rerun the rule.
The output already existed and none of its inputs had changed, so Snakemake kept the old table,
and DESeq2 then failed because the count matrix and the table listed different samples.

The lesson for module 7: Snakemake reruns a job when something it *tracks* changes. Python values
computed at parse time are not tracked. If a rule's output depends on a file, put the file in
`input:`, even when the rule gets the values some other way. `qc_summary` and `qc_report` do the
same, and `tests/test_stale_inputs.py` checks it by really running the rule, appending two samples,
and running it again:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="tests/test_stale_inputs.py" lines="30-54" >}}

`sample_table` is also the only `run:` block in the lab's pipelines. It is a few lines of pure
Python with no tool to call, which is the case `run:` is for.

### Switches and conditional includes {#tt-switches}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="13-25" >}}

Three booleans decide which parts of the workflow exist. Note the guard right after them: a config with
every switch off is an error, not a run that does nothing. The two string settings are checked
against their allowed values immediately, so `strandedness: dUTp` fails at parse time with the
allowed values in the message.

The Snakefile then includes rule files, one of them only when a switch is on:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/TTpipe.snakefile" lines="52-59" >}}

With `spike_in.enabled: false` (the default), `spike.smk` is never read and its rules do not exist.

### `if TRIM:` defines a rule, or doesn't {#tt-conditional-rules}

`include:` is not the only way to switch rules. Inside `processing.smk`, rules are defined inside
ordinary Python `if` blocks:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/processing.smk" lines="8-24" >}}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/processing.smk" lines="68-91" >}}

When `trim` is false, there is no `fastp` rule at all, and `star_reads()` hands STAR the raw FASTQs.
When it is true, `star_reads()` returns the trimmed paths, which only `fastp` can produce, so the
DAG gains one `fastp` job per sample. The test `test_trim_adds_fastp` checks exactly that: four more
jobs, all of them `fastp`.

Two small things in `fastp`: `TRIM_R.replace("{mate}", "1")` fills in one wildcard of a template by
hand and leaves `{sample}` for Snakemake, and both trimmed files are `temp()`, removed once STAR
has read them.

The same trick gives *variants* of a rule. `processing.smk` defines `scale_factors`,
`bigwig_sample` and `count_matrix` under `if not SPIKE_ENABLED:`, and `spike.smk` defines rules with
the same names for the spike-in case. Exactly one version exists in any run. Profiles key on rule
names, so one `set-resources: scale_factors:` entry covers both.

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/spike.smk" lines="90-113" >}}

Compare its input (the spike-in counts table) with the plain version's (the merged BAMs). The two
variants need different inputs, which is why this is two rules and not one rule with an `if` inside
`params`.

### Target functions {#tt-targets}

`rule all` in TTpipe is one line: `all_targets()`. The work is in `common.smk`:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="326-341" >}}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="356-387" >}}

- Each part of the workflow has its own function, and `all_targets()` adds them up according to
  the switches.
- Every path is built from a template defined once near the top of `common.smk` (`FASTQC_ZIP`,
  `BIGWIG_STRAND`, ...). The rules use the same templates as their outputs, so the target list and
  the rules cannot disagree about a filename.
- `stranded_targets()` is the subtle one. In an analysis-only run, the stranded bigWigs are not
  built in this run. The page is requested only if the files already exist on disk from an earlier
  run; otherwise it is skipped quietly. That is a target function deciding based on the file
  system at parse time, which is fine for *targets* but would be a mistake inside a rule's inputs.

### Wildcard constraints, including an empty one {#tt-wildcards}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/common.smk" lines="85-91" >}}

Same idea as MicroCPipe: each wildcard matches only the real names. The `or "NONE"` matters when
the list is empty (no GSEA collections): `"|".join([])` is the empty string, an empty pattern that
matches an empty wildcard value. `"NONE"` keeps the constraint a real pattern that no file uses.

`merge_bams` uses a rule-level constraint to let one rule make three files per condition:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/processing.smk" lines="241-269" >}}

`suffix = "|_forward|_reverse"` allows the empty string as one of the alternatives, so
`merged/DMSO.bam`, `merged/DMSO_forward.bam` and `merged/DMSO_reverse.bam` all come from this rule.
By default a wildcard has to match at least one character, so without the constraint the
all-reads BAM would have no rule. The input lambda then picks the right per-sample BAMs from the
suffix.

### Shell escaping in the real world {#tt-escaping}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/processing.smk" lines="271-301" >}}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/processing.smk" lines="303-329" >}}

Three escapes from module 4 in a few lines:

- `${{kv%%=*}}` is bash's `${kv%%=*}` (everything before the first `=`) with the braces doubled so
  Snakemake leaves them alone.
- `awk ... '$1==c {{print $3}}'` is the same rule for awk's braces.
- `'%s\\t%s\\n'` is written with two backslashes so the shell script contains `\t`, which `printf`
  turns into a tab. MicroCPipe's preseq fallback writes a single `\t`, so Python puts a literal tab
  character in the script; both work, but the doubled form keeps the command readable in `-p`
  output.

The `[ -n "$SF" ] || { ...; exit 1; }` line in `bigwig` is the opposite of MicroCPipe's preseq
fallback: here an empty scale factor is a real error, so the block writes a message and fails the
job on purpose.

`{PY}` in these commands is not a rule field. It is the module-level variable
`PY = "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python"` from the top of `processing.smk`; Snakemake fills shell
placeholders from the rule's fields first and then from global variables. It works, but the
linter flags it (see [conventions](conventions.qmd#lint)), and a reader looking for `PY` in the
rule will not find it.

### Params that must not be filled in {#tt-params}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/analysis.smk" lines="10-33" >}}

`deseq2` runs once for all comparisons and writes one CSV per comparison. The R script needs the
*pattern* `degs_{comparison}.csv`, with the braces still in it, to know where to write. A plain
string param would be formatted with the job's wildcards and fail (this rule has no `{comparison}`
wildcard). Wrapping it in `lambda wildcards: DEGS` turns that off: Snakemake does not format the
value a params function returns.

The neighboring rule shows a constraint from module 2 that is easy to forget:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/analysis.smk" lines="59-77" >}}

All outputs of a rule must have the same wildcards. The ranked list has `{comparison}` only; the
fgsea result has `{collection}` and `{comparison}`. So the ranked list gets its own rule.

### Inputs that depend on the run mode {#tt-run-mode}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="workflows/rules/report.smk" lines="16-44" >}}

The QC report reads different files in a processing-only, analysis-only or full run. Its input
function returns a dictionary, and `qc_report` uses `unpack(qc_report_inputs)` so each key becomes a
named input (`{input.sample_qc}`, `{input.scale}`). In a report-only run, `_qc_summary_data_inputs`
lists only files that already exist, so nothing is built.

### Resources in profiles, and one launcher difference {#tt-launcher}

The resource story is MicroCPipe's: rules declare only `threads:`, and every rule has a
`set-threads` and `set-resources` entry in each profile. The local profile's comments are honest
about where the numbers come from:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="profiles/local/config.yaml" lines="1-15" >}}

The launcher is *not* the same, though:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="TTpipe.sh" lines="58-65" >}}

TTpipe's launcher activates the venv, the thing MicroCPipe's launcher deliberately avoids. TTpipe
copes on the inside instead: every script is run as `$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/python` (`PY` in
`processing.smk`), and the comments in `report.smk` say why ("the launcher's venv bin/ is first on
PATH in cluster jobs"). Python tools inside the conda environments can still hit the problem
MicroCPipe describes when an environment path is long enough for conda to rewrite their first
line. Two other differences from MicroCPipe: TTpipe's SLURM
profiles have no `cores: 100` line, and the launcher has no check for unedited `<placeholder>`
values. If you run TTpipe on SLURM, check a `star_align` log for the thread count it actually used.

### Tests that assert job counts {#tt-tests}

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" lines="26-47" >}}

`dry_run()` runs `snakemake -n` with the main config plus an overlay and optional `--config`
overrides. `jobs()` turns the "Job stats" table into a dictionary. With those two helpers, each
test is a statement about the DAG:

{{< snippet repo="ttpipe" file="tests/test_dryrun.py" lines="83-108" >}}

These tests check *differences*: turning on `trim` adds exactly four jobs and all of them are
`fastp`; per-sample tracks add twelve `bigwig_sample` jobs; turning off the report removes exactly
two. A test like that keeps passing when someone adds an unrelated rule, and fails when a switch
starts pulling in more (or less) than it should. The same file also feeds broken samplesheets and
configs to a dry run and checks the error message, so the parse-time checks in `common.smk` are
tested too.

## What you would change {#tt-change}

- **Stop activating the venv in `TTpipe.sh` and `unlock.sh`**, as MicroCPipe does, and add the
  `cores: 100` line and the placeholder check from MicroCPipe's profiles and launcher. The three
  launchers started from one pattern and have drifted.
- **Add `conda:` to the four spike-in rules that call `{PY}` without one** (`spike_reference`,
  `spike_summary`, the spike-in `scale_factors`, `spike_size_factors`). The scripts use only the
  standard library, so `$CONDA_PREFIX` falling back to the launcher's base environment works today,
  but it depends on how the launcher set up the shell.
- **Rename `PY` and `SCRIPTS` into `params:`** (`params: py=PY`), so each rule says what it uses.
- **Move a few small rules to `localrules:`.** `sample_table` writes a few lines of text; on SLURM it
  is still a queued job.

## Exercises for the curious {#tt-exercises}

1. You want to add RSeQC's `infer_experiment.py` as an optional strandedness check. List every file
   you would touch.
2. Delete `config["samplesheet"]` from the input of `sample_table`, run the pipeline, add two
   samples, and run it again. What happens, and which rule fails?
3. Why are `scale_factors` and `count_matrix` defined twice, under opposite `if`s, instead of once
   with an `if` inside the rule?
4. The tests count jobs from `snakemake -n`. Name one kind of bug these tests cannot catch.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Short answers

1. The config (a switch, off by default); `common.smk` (an output template and a line in
   `processing_targets()` behind the switch); a rule in `processing.smk` (with `conda:` and
   `threads:`); an env file in `envs/` if no existing one has RSeQC; a `set-threads`/`set-resources`
   entry in every profile; a dry-run test that the switch adds one job per sample; and the docs.
   If the QC report should show it, `report.smk` and `qc_report.py` too.
2. `sample_table` does not rerun, because its output exists and nothing it tracks has changed. The
   count matrix is rebuilt (its inputs changed), so `deseq2` gets a matrix with six samples and a
   table with four, and fails with "sample names differ between the count matrix and the sample
   table". That is the bug the comment describes.
3. The two versions need different *inputs* (merged BAMs, or the spike-in counts table), and inputs
   decide the DAG. A single rule would need an input function that switches, plus params that
   switch, plus a shell command that switches. Two small rules are easier to read and to test, and
   because they share a name the profiles need no change.
4. Anything that happens when a tool runs: wrong flags, a wrong `samtools -f` strand mask, a script
   that crashes on real data. A dry run never executes a command. The unit tests in `tests/`
   (`test_processing_scripts.py`, `test_stranded_signal.py`, ...) cover some scripts on small
   synthetic inputs; the tools themselves were checked on real data on the cluster
   (`docs/validation.qmd`).
:::
